title: Al-'Alaq: the one who forbids
hookLine: the man who forbids a servant to pray, and the command to bow and draw near (96:9–19)
tomorrow: At-Tin: the fig and the olive

lines: WHAT SHOULD THE ONE PRAYING DO?
cards: The Ka'bah in Mecca, in the early years. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is praying there in the open, bowing, then putting his forehead on the ground. A powerful man of Quraysh is watching, and he's furious.

He tells his friends: if I see Muhammad with his face in the dust again, I'll step on his neck. The rest of Surah al-'Alaq, after the first five verses, is about this man, and about what the one praying should do.

teach.b: The surah turns from the pen to a warning: truly, the human being oversteps when he sees himself as self-sufficient.

Then: have you seen the one who forbids a servant when he prays? The surah doesn't name him. Commentators, and a hadith in Sahih Muslim, identify him as Abu Jahl, a leading opponent of the Prophet in Mecca.

The hadith says he came forward to carry out his threat, then suddenly drew back, shielding himself with his hands. Asked why, he said he'd seen between himself and the Prophet a trench of fire, and terror, and wings.
The surah asks him questions: what if the one praying is rightly guided? What if he commands goodness? Doesn't he know that Allah sees?
Then the last verse tells the one praying what to do. In Pickthall's translation: Nay!
Obey not thou him. But prostrate thyself, and draw near unto Allah. Not fight.
Not argue. Not hide. Bow down, and come closer.
It's counted among the verses of prostration, though the schools of law differ on it.
And it lines up with a hadith in Muslim: the closest a servant is to his Lord is while in prostration.
The lowest position of the body is the nearest point to Allah. The man who wanted to push a face into the dust didn't understand: that's exactly where the nearness is.
That closes a week that began with the quake and an atom of good, and moved through the earth's report, the clear proof, sincerity, the Night of Power, and now the cave and its first surah, whole.

how: When Muslims recite or hear 96:19 many perform a prostration of recitation (sajdat al-tilawah); in the daily prayers, the prostration is often called the moment of greatest nearness to Allah.

games.q: you're praying in the open, and a powerful man has sworn to stop you. what does the surah tell you to do?
o: don't obey him; prostrate, and draw near
games.why: the last verse: nay! obey not thou him. but prostrate thyself, and draw near (96:19).

practice: If you pray, make one prostration now, forehead to the ground, and stay a few breaths longer than usual, drawing near.
If you don't, lower your head gently toward your knees or your hands, and let your whole body get small and still. Feel what it's like to go low on purpose, with nothing to prove down there.

wordCard.voice: Al-'Alaq. The clinging thing, and the surah that ends: don't obey the one who forbids; bow down, and draw near. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: and draw near; the last word of Surah 96.

carryVoice: Your line: bow and draw near. When shame comes for what you value, the answer here is lower and closer. A week complete, day one hundred eighty-two.
